title_en: Inwang jesaekdo (Scene of Inwangsan Mountain After Rain) by Jeong Seon
key_facts: Jeong Seon (1676–1759), also known by his pen name Gyeomjae, painted Inwangjesaekdo (Mount Inwang After Rain) in 1751. The inscription dates the work to the latter part of the intercalary fifth lunar month.|The painting depicts Mount Inwang in Seoul after rainfall, with dark, rain-soaked rocky peaks rising above mist-filled valleys and wooded slopes.|Inwangjesaekdo is a celebrated example of jingyeong sansuhwa (true-view landscape painting), which takes recognizable Korean places as its starting point while creatively reshaping them through composition and brushwork, rather than merely reproducing inherited landscape conventions. This does not imply that Chinese painters never depicted real places.|Jeong Seon lived near Mount Inwang for much of his life, developing a close familiarity with the mountain and its surrounding landscape.|Jeong Seon uses repeated, densely layered strokes of dark ink to depict the massive rock faces, especially the prominent Chimabawi formation, creating a sense of weight, rugged texture, and rain-soaked stone.|Areas of unpainted paper and pale ink washes suggest mist drifting between the mountains, while the contrast with the dark rocks makes the peaks appear to emerge from the damp atmosphere.|The foreground includes clusters of trees, distinctive pine forms, and small buildings partly concealed among the foliage, emphasizing the enormous scale of the mountain.|The composition combines different viewpoints: the foreground buildings appear to be seen from above, while the towering rocky peaks suggest a viewpoint from below, heightening the mountain's dramatic presence.|Although based on a real landscape, the painting reorganizes and emphasizes geographical features rather than reproducing them with photographic accuracy. Scholars have noted the exaggerated scale of the rocks and proposed connections to nearby valleys.|The exact reason for the painting's creation is unknown. Art historian Choe Wan-su interpreted it as a possible wish for the recovery of Jeong Seon's friend Yi Byeong-yeon, while other interpretations concern a possible commission or the commemoration of Mount Inwang's scenery.|Art historian Oh Ju-seok used rainfall records from the Seungjeongwon Ilgi to propose that the painting was made on the afternoon of the twenty-fifth day of the intercalary fifth lunar month in 1751. This is a scholarly hypothesis rather than a confirmed completion date, and the identity of the house depicted in the foreground also remains uncertain.

title_en: "Korean Traditional Wrestling" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: Kim Hong-do's Ssireum (Korean Traditional Wrestling) is a late-eighteenth-century Joseon genre painting from his Album of Genre Paintings, a collection of twenty-five scenes depicting everyday activities such as work, education, and leisure.|Two wrestlers grapple in the center, surrounded by spectators in two curved groups that form a roughly circular composition and leave an open space focused on the contest.|A toffee vendor stands on the left carrying a tray of sweets. Unlike the spectators watching the match, he faces away from the action, while his position helps complete the circular arrangement.|Several pairs of shoes lie on the ground to the right of the wrestlers, visually narrowing the open space and balancing the groups of spectators.|The spectators display varied expressions and gestures, including smiling, leaning forward, and sitting casually, allowing viewers to sense the excitement and different reactions surrounding the match.|Kim Hong-do uses economical, expressive brushstrokes to capture the figures' movements and facial expressions, while rougher strokes suggest the texture of their cotton clothing.|The broad, rounded faces and circular eyes of the figures are characteristic features of Kim Hong-do's genre paintings, and the largely empty background keeps attention on the people and their interactions.|Ssireum is a traditional Korean wrestling sport in which two competitors grip each other's cloth belts (satba) and attempt to make the opponent touch the ground with a body part other than the feet, using balance, strength, and technique. The exact rules have varied across time and regional traditions.|The painting shows one wrestler lifting a leg during the struggle, capturing a moment of physical tension and movement without establishing which competitor will win.|Ssireum has a long history in Korea, with wrestling scenes appearing in Goguryeo tomb murals. During the Joseon dynasty, people from different social backgrounds enjoyed wrestling, although the status of individual figures in this painting cannot be determined from their appearance alone.|Ssireum was associated with seasonal celebrations such as Dano, Baekjung, and Chuseok. However, the painting contains no conclusive evidence identifying a particular holiday or occasion.

title_en: "A Village School" from the Album of Genre Paintings by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: The painting depicts a scene in a Joseon village school, or seodang, where a young student sits crying in front of a teacher while other students gather around them.|The crying student sits with his back partly turned toward the viewer and appears to be adjusting his trouser legs. The National Museum of Korea interprets the scene as suggesting that he has just been struck with a switch.|The teacher wears a square-shaped traditional hat called a banggeon and Confucian-style robes. He looks toward the crying child with an expression interpreted by the museum as sympathetic.|The surrounding students respond in different ways: some appear amused, while others watch the crying child with curiosity. Their varied expressions and gestures create humor and a sense of lively interaction.|Kim Hong-do arranges the figures in a roughly circular composition against an almost empty background, using their gestures and expressions to direct attention to the crying student and teacher.|The painting uses concise, expressive brushwork to distinguish the characters and convey the atmosphere of the classroom.|The Digital Ansan Cultural Encyclopedia identifies iron-wire lines (cheolseonmyo) and nail-head-and-rat-tail lines (jeongduseomimyo) among the figure-drawing techniques used in the painting. The latter technique begins with a firm stroke that gradually tapers to a fine point.|In Joseon village schools, gangdok was a method of learning classical texts through repeated reading aloud, memorization, and explanation. Teachers assigned passages according to each student's progress.|Students were assessed through a practice known as gang (講), in which they recited previously studied passages and explained their meaning. Historical accounts describe corporal punishment for students who failed such assessments.|The National Institute of Korean History suggests that the crying student in Kim Hong-do's painting may have been punished after failing a recitation assessment. This is a historically informed interpretation, not a documented explanation of the particular child's circumstances.

title_en: Portrait of Kang Se-hwang, autograph version
key_facts: Kang Se-hwang (1713–1791) was a prominent Joseon scholar-painter, calligrapher, art critic, and government official whose artistic and scholarly identities are reflected in this portrait.|The portrait is traditionally identified as a self-portrait made in 1782, when Kang was seventy years old according to traditional Korean age reckoning, as recorded in its inscription.|Self-portraits were uncommon in Joseon Korea, where portraits were often created to commemorate individuals and preserve their likenesses for descendants and ancestral rites. Kang Se-hwang's portrait and Yun Du-seo's self-portrait are notable surviving examples.|Kang portrays himself seated in a full-length composition, wearing a black gauze official’s hat (osamo) with loose, pale jade-blue informal robes and a narrow red cord belt (sejodae) decorated with gold pigment.|Official heritage commentary interprets the unusual combination of an official hat and informal robe as expressing Kang’s public achievements and his attachment to scholarly life outside the court.|The face is carefully rendered with fine lines describing wrinkles, subtle shading around the eyes and cheeks, and a long white beard. Official heritage commentary relates aspects of this facial modeling to Western-influenced techniques.|Kang's hands are concealed within his voluminous sleeves, while the carefully arranged folds of the robe emphasize his composed, seated posture.|Kang’s inscription on both sides of the figure describes his appearance, learning, artistic identity, and aspirations; it also identifies his sobriquet Nojuk (露竹) and states that he painted the portrait and composed the inscription himself.|In the inscription, Kang contrasts his official position at court with his inner attachment to mountains and forests, expressing the tension between public service and the private ideals of a scholar.|Kang Se-hwang entered government service later in life and subsequently participated in royal portrait production under King Jeongjo. He was also an influential teacher and mentor to the painter Kim Hong-do.
source_note: e뮤지엄에서 작품 기본정보 확인. 국가유산 지식이음·국가유산포털에서 자찬문, 복식의 의미와 얼굴의 명암 표현 확인. 작품 이미지에서 오사모·옥빛 옷·붉은 띠·가려진 손 확인. 한국민족문화대백과사전·우리역사넷에서 작가 생애와 김홍도와의 관계 참고. [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 본 데이터는 1782년 강세황의 70세 자화상(소장품번호: 구 10562)을 대상으로 한다. 검은 오사모와 옥색 야복을 착용하고 있으며, 화면 양쪽에 자찬문이 있는 작품이다. 보물 제590호에는 이 자화상과 이명기가 1783년에 제작한 71세 관복본 《강세황 초상》이 함께 포함되어 있으므로 두 작품을 혼동하지 않는다. 특히 이명기 초상은 정식 관복과 흉배를 착용한 모습으로 구분한다. 또한 국립중앙박물관 소장품번호 덕수3069의 《강세황 초상》은 종이에 그린 별개의 관복 차림 정면상(50.9 × 31.5cm)이므로 본 자화상 및 이명기 초상과 혼동하지 않는다. 작품 식별 시 제목이나 보물 지정번호만으로 판단하지 않고 소장품번호, 제작 연도, 복식, 화면 구성 및 자찬문 유무를 함께 확인한다.

key_facts: Kim Jeong-hui (1786–1856), also known as Chusa and Wandang, created Sehando (A Wintry Scene) in 1844 while living in exile on Jeju Island.|He made the painting for his disciple Yi Sang-jeok (1804–1865), a government interpreter who continued to obtain and send him valuable books from Beijing despite Kim's loss of political standing.|Kim’s handwritten postscript praises Yi Sang-jeok for remaining loyal before and after Kim’s exile and explains the gift through the Confucian image of evergreen trees enduring winter.|The title Sehando (歲寒圖) refers to the cold season and draws on a passage from the Analects of Confucius about recognizing the endurance of pines and cypresses only after the weather turns cold.|The painting depicts a small, simply drawn house among sparsely rendered trees and extensive blank space; its evergreen imagery evokes Yi’s steadfast loyalty, while the austere setting can also suggest the isolation of exile.|Kim uses dry brushwork (galpil), restrained ink, and extensive blank space to create an austere scene without elaborate decorative detail.|The painting exemplifies the ideals of Joseon literati painting, which valued the expression of personal character and inner meaning (saui) and the close relationship between calligraphy and painting (seohwa ilchi).|The painting bears the title Sehando, a dedication to Yi Sang-jeok using his sobriquet Useon (藕船), Kim's pen name Wandang (阮堂), and seals bearing the names Jeonghui (正喜) and Wandang (阮堂).|Yi Sang-jeok brought the painting to Beijing in 1845, where sixteen Qing scholars contributed poems and commentaries, extending the work's significance beyond the original exchange between teacher and disciple.|The surviving handscroll combines Kim's 1844 painting and postscript with later writings, including an introductory inscription by Kim Jun-hak dated 1914, additional notes by Qing scholars and Kim Jun-hak, and subsequent commentaries by Korean scholars Oh Se-chang, Yi Si-yeong, and Jeong In-bo.

title_ko: 끝없이 펼쳐진 강과 산 (이인문 필 강산무진도)
title_en: Rivers and Mountains without End (Gangsan Mujindo)
key_facts: The painting is an exceptionally long horizontal handscroll made from five joined pieces of silk, allowing an expansive landscape to unfold continuously as the viewer moves along it.|The landscape is an imaginative composition rather than a depiction of one identifiable geographical location. The National Museum of Korea describes it as an ideal world in which people live in harmony with enduring nature.|The long handscroll is traditionally viewed gradually from right to left, revealing shifting scenery from low mountains and calm waters to rugged peaks and dramatic terrain; this unfolding sequence rewards close observation rather than a single fixed view.|Yi In-mun employs an elevated, distant viewpoint, arranging mountains, rivers, cliffs, valleys, and plains into a panoramic landscape with striking changes in scale and scenery.|The mountains are rendered with varied texture strokes, or junbeop, including axe-cut strokes (bubyeokjun) and Mi-dot strokes (mijeomjun), creating contrasting surfaces and a strong sense of depth.|Carefully controlled brushwork, delicate colors, and densely detailed natural forms, including numerous pine trees, contribute to the landscape's rich and varied visual character.|Small figures throughout the landscape travel, work, and pursue everyday activities, while villages, markets, houses, pavilions, temples, and fortified settlements show diverse human life amid the mountains and waterways.|The landscape includes houses, villages, markets, fortified settlements, pavilions, and Buddhist temples, placing diverse forms of human settlement within an expansive natural setting.|Boats and ships appear along waterways, while carts and other forms of land transportation suggest the movement of people and goods across the imagined landscape.|The painting also includes pulley-operated mechanisms and water-related devices. Art historian Kho Youn-hee discusses these features in relation to late-Joseon interest in practical technology and productive activity, while their precise functions should not be assumed without further evidence.|Art historian Kho Youn-hee interprets the transportation, markets, and technology as part of a vision of an ideal society in which commerce and productive activity coexist with magnificent nature; the National Museum of Korea also emphasizes harmony with the enduring natural world. Neither reading establishes the painter’s documented intention.|The title Gangsan Mujindo (Rivers and Mountains without End) appears on a label attached to the scroll, but the National Museum of Korea explains that this was not a title assigned when Yi In-mun originally created the painting.|An artist-related seal at the end of the scroll reads 李寅文文郁道人也, referring to Yi In-mun and his literary name Munuk (文郁).|Seals reading Chusa (秋史) and Chusa jinjang (秋史珍藏) at the front and back of the scroll indicate that it was once owned by the scholar and calligrapher Kim Jeong-hui (1786–1856).

title_en: Chuseongbudo (Theme of Chuseongbu, Sounds of Autumn) by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: Kim Hong-do dated the painting to the third day after the winter solstice of the eulchuk year (1805), signing it with his pen name Dan-gu (丹邱). He was sixty-one years old according to traditional Korean age reckoning.|The painting is generally regarded as Kim Hong-do's last known dated work, although his exact year of death is uncertain and the designation does not establish that it was his final painting.|The work is a pictorial interpretation (siuido) of Chuseongbu (Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn), a prose-poem by the Song-dynasty scholar Ouyang Xiu (1007–1072).|Kim Hong-do transcribed the entire Chinese text of Chuseongbu in his own calligraphy on the left side of the painting, combining literature, calligraphy, and painting in a single work.|In Chuseongbu, Ouyang Xiu hears a mysterious sound coming from the southwest while reading at night and asks a servant boy to investigate its source.|The text compares the sound to rushing waves, sudden wind and rain, clanging metal, and soldiers advancing toward battle, transforming an invisible sound into vivid sensory imagery.|The servant boy reports that the moon and stars shine brightly, the Milky Way stretches across the sky, no human voices can be heard, and the sound comes from among the trees.|Ouyang Xiu identifies the sound as the voice of autumn and reflects on the seasonal decline of plants and trees, human aging, and the worries that exhaust the mind and body.|The literary work ends with the servant boy falling asleep while the chirping of insects around the walls seems to accompany Ouyang Xiu's sighs.|The painting depicts the moment when the servant boy points toward the trees after investigating the mysterious sound, while Ouyang Xiu sits inside a Chinese-style thatched house and is visible through a large round window.|Two cranes in the courtyard stretch their necks and open their beaks as if responding to the wind. These birds are pictorial details rather than figures mentioned in Ouyang Xiu's original text.|Windblown deciduous trees, scattered fallen leaves, a full moon, a bamboo-surrounded thatched house, and a sparsely vegetated autumn mountain establish the setting of a chilly night.|Mountains and hills on both sides frame the central house and courtyard, while a slightly elevated viewpoint emphasizes the main narrative scene.|Dark tones, dry-brush strokes (galpil), and thin, irregularly forked trees suggest the chill and sound of wind through the autumn landscape, translating the literary work’s atmosphere and emotions into visual form.|A white-lettered oval seal reading Giuyuja (騎牛游子) appears on the left side of the painting, alongside Kim Hong-do's handwritten transcription of the literary work.|According to the Korea Heritage Service's commentary, Kim Hong-do quoted the phrase 'a hundred worries affect the heart' (百憂感其心) from Chuseongbu in a letter written in 1805 to a recipient called Kim Saengwon. This provides historical context for interpretations connecting the painting to Kim's concerns in later life, but does not prove his specific motive for creating it.

title_en: Woman Carrying a Baby on Her Back, by Shin Yun-bok
key_facts: The painting shows a young woman carrying a small child on her back against a largely empty background, directing attention to the figures and their clothing.|The woman wears a short, closely fitted jacket, a voluminous skirt, and an elaborate wig (gache), fashions associated with women in late Joseon.|The woman's jacket is so short that part of her breasts is visible. The National Museum of Korea interprets the child on her back as evoking maternal affection, although their actual relationship is not documented.|The woman's appearance resembles that of a gisaeng, a female entertainer, according to the museum's interpretation, but her social status cannot be established from her clothing alone.|The scholar Yi Deok-mu criticized short jackets, wide skirts, and extravagant wigs, describing their association with female entertainers; this reflects a contemporary critical perspective rather than proving the woman’s social identity.|At the lower right, Shin Yun-bok inscribed his pen name Hyewon and stamped a seal generally read Waganun (臥看雲), “reclining and watching the clouds”; some publications differ in reading its final character.|A lengthy inscription in the empty space was written by a commentator using the name Buseol Geosa, whose identity and relationship to the painter remain unknown.|The inscription recalls how the Song-dynasty poet Su Shi, also known as Su Dongpo, composed the poem Xu Liren Xing (A Sequel to the Song of the Beauties) in response to a painting attributed to the Tang-dynasty painter Zhou Fang.|The painting described in the literary tradition depicted a palace woman seen from behind as she stretched and yawned; the original painting has not been securely identified with a surviving work.|Buseol Geosa draws particular attention to the small child carried on the woman's back, noting that such a figure was absent from Zhou Fang's painting.|The commentator praises the woman's gentle elegance and the painting's sinun (神韻), or expressive spirit and resonance, suggesting a quality beyond technical brushwork.|By invoking Zhou Fang's painting and Su Shi's poetry, the inscription places this work within a tradition of appreciating painting through literary comparison.

key_facts: Chaekgado is a form of Korean bookshelf painting within the broader chaekgeori tradition, depicting books, scholarly implements, treasured objects, and sometimes imagined possessions associated with learning and aspiration.|King Jeongjo valued books and scholarship and commissioned bookshelf paintings for the royal court; chaekgeori later spread beyond courtly and scholar-official circles.|This particular screen depicts numerous stacks of books, many with patterned covers or cases, alongside brushes, vessels, and decorative objects.|A pair of round spectacles rests on paper above stacked books, showing how practical objects associated with reading could appear among scholarly possessions.|A cut watermelon appears in one compartment; in the broader chaekgeori tradition, fruits with many seeds, such as watermelons, could symbolize wishes for numerous descendants.|A dish holds clusters of yellow, textured forms that may represent Buddha's hand citrons (bulsugam), a fruit motif associated with good fortune in chaekgeori paintings; the identification in this screen remains uncertain.|The screen arranges open shelves, compartments, and closed doors in varied depths, using perspective and shading to suggest a three-dimensional cabinet.|In the second panel of this screen, a cabinet door decorated with a landscape painting is shown partly open.|The partly open painted door and the cord and rectangular object apparently hanging from its lock exemplify trompe-l’œil, an illusionistic technique that makes painted things seem physically present.|In a 2025 scholarly publication, Yi Jeong-eun identifies this screen as a late eighteenth-century work, although its exact production date remains unknown.|In a 2025 study, Yi Jeong-eun compares Joseon chaekgado with eighteenth-century Chinese bookshelf paintings, noting similarities in objects, compositions, and illusionistic devices without establishing direct copying of a particular Chinese work.
source_note: e뮤지엄·국립중앙박물관에서 건희 4123의 이미지와 기물 확인. 국립박물관문화재단·우리역사넷에서 책가도의 역사와 상징 참고. 이정은(2025)에서 편년 추정·눈속임 표현·중국 책장 그림 비교, 신미란(2010)에서 불수감 도상 참고. [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 다른 책가도 소장품과 혼동하지 않는다. 노란 과일의 정체, 제작 연도, 중국 그림과의 직접 모방 관계를 단정하지 않는다.

title_en: Painting of a Dog and Puppies
key_facts: Painting of a Dog and Puppies, also known as Mogyeondo (Mother Dog and Puppies), is a sixteenth-century Joseon painting by Yi Am (1499–?), whose exact year of death remains unknown.|One light-colored puppy rests with closed eyes on the mother’s back, while two others nestle beneath her body in positions suggesting nursing; their overlapping forms create an intimate, affectionate scene, although actual feeding cannot be confirmed.|The mother dog turns her head to the left and wears a red collar with a golden bell, suggesting that she was cared for by humans, although her original owner is unknown.|Yi Am depicts the dogs’ rounded bodies and fur with subtle, softly blended transitions between light and dark, allowing color to merge without relying entirely on hard outlines.|The background tree, with its dark trunk and loosely brushed foliage, is rendered more simply than the dogs, drawing attention to the animals and their contrasting poses.|The dogs' overlapping bodies, relaxed postures, and attentive expressions create a sense of warmth and closeness, inviting viewers to appreciate an intimate moment of animal life.|The painting belongs to yeongmohwa, the Korean tradition of painting birds and animals, and demonstrates the genre's attention to the forms and behavior of living creatures.|Art historians associate Yi Am’s animal paintings more broadly with the ink-wash, boneless-style tradition (sumuk molgol), which suggests forms through washes and shading rather than firm outlines; this does not establish a technique for every part of this particular work.|According to the Veritable Records of King Injong, Yi Am and Yi Sang-jwa were recommended by the Royal Secretariat to paint a posthumous portrait of King Jungjong, indicating Yi Am's recognized artistic skill.|Yi Am's distinctive and gentle approach to animal painting is regarded as an important development in Korean art history, with related traditions appearing in the work of later animal painters such as Kim Sik and Byeon Sang-byeok.
source_note: e뮤지엄·국립중앙박물관에서 동물의 털 표현과 배경 나무 묘사 확인. 소장품 이미지에서 강아지들의 자세와 목줄·방울 확인. 한국민족문화대백과사전 「영모화」에서 이암의 수묵몰골풍 관련 평가 참고. 뉴스컬처에서 정서적 해석 참고. [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 제작 연도·작가 사망 연도는 미상이다. 수묵몰골풍은 화가의 동물화 전반에 대한 설명이며, 실제 수유·소유주·사육 환경은 단정하지 않는다.

title_en: Plants and Insects, Attributed to Shin Saimdang
key_facts: Jeon Shin Saimdang Pil Chochungdo is traditionally attributed to Shin Saimdang (1504–1551); the attribution term jeon (傳) indicates a handed-down attribution rather than conclusively authenticated authorship.|The painting is one of eight panels associated with a folding screen of plants and insects. The image shown here depicts the panel commonly known as Watermelons and Field Mice.|Two large dark-green watermelons dominate the lower composition, while a smaller developing fruit hangs from a curving vine that connects the fruit to leaves and blossoms above.|The watermelon on the right has an opening that reveals pale and reddish flesh and seeds, providing a striking contrast with its dark rind.|Two small field mice appear below the opened watermelon near scattered reddish fruit fragments, suggesting feeding activity without proving that both are biting directly into the fruit.|Two butterflies with contrasting wing colors and patterns appear in the upper part of the painting, one reddish and the other predominantly pale with dark markings.|Two reddish dianthus flowers, commonly called pinks, rise along the right side of the painting, adding a vertical accent to the spreading watermelon vines.|The contrast between large rounded watermelons below and small mice, flowers, and butterflies above creates a balanced composition with varied scale and lively movement.|The National Museum of Korea highlights the painting's delicate brush lines, vivid coloring, and stable composition as distinctive qualities of its depiction of watermelons, mice, and butterflies.|Chochungdo literally means a painting of grasses and insects. The genre depicts small plants, flowers, insects, and sometimes other animals, bringing close attention to familiar forms of nature.|In traditional symbolic readings, the watermelon’s numerous seeds and spreading vines may suggest fertility, offspring, and continuing growth; these are possible interpretations, not documented intentions of the painter.|The National Museum of Korea explains that paintings of plants and insects attributed to Shin Saimdang were frequently adapted into embroidery in later periods. This does not establish that this panel was originally designed as an embroidery pattern.|According to the National Museum of Korea's curatorial commentary, paintings of plants and insects attributed to Shin Saimdang were admired by eighteenth-century literati and viewed in connection with her reputation and her son, the scholar Yi I. Their later appreciation is historically significant but does not independently establish the painting's authorship.
source_note: e뮤지엄·국립중앙박물관에서 8폭 병풍 관련 정보, 작품 이미지와 자수본 활용 해설 확인. 한국민족문화대백과사전에서 초충도 장르 참고. 조규희(2013)에서 후대 귀속·수용사, 관련 블로그에서 수박·들쥐 등의 상징 해석 참고. [AI 도슨트 운영 메모] 현재 이미지는 수박·들쥐 한 폭이다. 신사임당 친필·제작 연도·다산 상징의 제작 의도를 단정하지 않는다. 후대 자수 활용을 원래 제작 목적으로 해석하지 않는다.
